title.en: Beyond AB — Core BC Topics Overview

body.en: AP Calculus BC contains the entire AP Calculus AB curriculum plus four major mathematical pillars: Advanced Integration Techniques, Extended Differential Equations & Numerical Methods, Planar Parametric & Polar Calculus, and Infinite Sequences & Power Series. Mastering this 'BC Delta' accounts for approximately 40% of the total exam and is essential for earning a score of 5.

blocks.heading: Level 1 · Foundations — The Advanced Integration & Numerical Approximation Framework

body.en: In Unit 6BC, integration extends beyond \(u\)-substitution to products of algebraic and transcendental functions via Integration by Parts, rational expressions with factorable denominators via Partial Fraction Decomposition, and integrands with unbounded intervals or vertical asymptotes via Improper Integrals.

label.en: ● Analytical Foundations: Integration by Parts & Euler's Method

body.en:
1. Integration by Parts Formula: Directly derived from the Product Rule \(\frac{d}{dx}[uv] = u'v + uv'\). Integrating both sides gives: \[ \int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du. \] Use the LIATE hierarchy to choose \(u\): Logarithmic, Inverse trigonometric, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential.

2. Euler's Method Iteration: A numerical algorithm for approximating solutions to initial value problems \(\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)\) with \(y(x_0) = y_0\) and step size \(\Delta x\): \[ x_{n+1} = x_n + \Delta x, \qquad y_{n+1} = y_n + f(x_n, y_n)\Delta x. \]

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Beyond AB — Core BC Topics Overview)

body.en:
Why Successive Multipliers & Harmonic Average Speed Work: If a quantity \(Q_0\) undergoes a percentage change \(p\%\) followed by \(q\%\), the compound multiplier is the product of individual scale factors:

\[ Q_{\text{final}} = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\!\left(1 + \frac{q}{100}\right) = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p + q}{100} + \frac{pq}{10000}\right) \]

Notice the cross term \(\dfrac{pq}{10000}\): an increase of \(p\%\) followed by a decrease of \(p\%\) yields \(Q_0\bigl(1 - (p/100)^2\bigr) < Q_0\). Similarly, traveling equal distance \(d\) at speeds \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) takes total time \(T = \frac{d}{v_1} + \frac{d}{v_2}\), so average speed is the harmonic mean \(v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{2d}{d/v_1 + d/v_2} = \dfrac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\).

label.en: Level 1 (Foundations) — Worked Example · Tabular Integration & LIATE Protocol

body.en:
Problem: Evaluate the indefinite integral \(\int x^2 e^{3x}\,dx\) using the Tabular Method.

Step 1 · Identify \(u\) and \(dv\): \(u = x^2\) (Algebraic, differentiates to 0) and \(dv = e^{3x}\,dx\) (Exponential, repeatedly integrates).

Step 2 · Construct the Differentiation & Integration Table:
• Row 0: \((+) \quad x^2 \qquad e^{3x}\)
• Row 1: \((-) \quad 2x \qquad \frac{1}{3}e^{3x}\)
• Row 2: \((+) \quad 2 \quad\quad \frac{1}{9}e^{3x}\)
• Row 3: \((-) \quad 0 \quad\quad \frac{1}{27}e^{3x}\)

Step 3 · Multiply Diagonals: \[ \int x^2 e^{3x}\,dx = x^2\left(\frac{1}{3}e^{3x}\right) - 2x\left(\frac{1}{9}e^{3x}\right) + 2\left(\frac{1}{27}e^{3x}\right) + C. \] Factor out \(e^{3x}\): \[ = \mathbf{\frac{e^{3x}}{27}\left(9x^2 - 6x + 2\right) + C}. \]

label.en: Worked Example \(B\) — Beyond AB — Core BC Topics Overview (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): Consider the function represented by the graph of \( f(x) \) below. What is the value of the definite integral \( \int_{0}^{4} f(x) \, dx \)?

Step-by-Step Solution: The definite integral \( \int_{0}^{4} f(x) \, dx \) represents the area under the curve \( f(x) \) from \( x=0 \) to \( x=4 \). The graph of \( f(x) \) from \( x=0 \) to \( x=4 \) forms a triangle with a base of 4 units (from 0 to 4 on the x-axis) and a height of 6 units (the value of \( f(x) \) at \( x=0 \)). The area of a triangle is given by \( \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} \). Therefore, the area is \( \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 6 = 12 \).

label.en: ⚠️ Common Exam Traps — Beyond AB — Core BC Topics Overview

body.en:
1. Adding Successive Percentages or Averaging Speeds Arithmetically: On College Board AP Calculus BC, a \(20\%\) discount followed by a \(20\%\) increase gives \(0.80 \times 1.20 = 0.96\) (a net \(4\%\) loss, not \(0\%\)). Likewise, average speed for a round trip at \(40\) and \(60\text{ km/h}\) is \(\dfrac{2(40)(60)}{100} = 48\text{ km/h}\), never \(50\text{ km/h}\).

2. Failing to Flip the Inequality Sign When Multiplying/Dividing by a Negative: In \(-2x + 5 \le 7\), dividing by \(-2\) strictly reverses \(\le\) to \(\ge\).

caption.en: Error Diagnosis — Common Student Traps vs. Exam-Board Method (Beyond AB — Core BC Topics Overview)

rows.en: The \(25\%\) reduction applies to the larger base \(1.25 Q_0\), not \(Q_0\).
Dividing by a negative number reverses order on the real number line.
Flip the inequality symbol whenever multiplying or dividing by a negative: \(x < -4\).
Computing round-trip average speed as \(\frac{v_1 + v_2}{2}\)
Time spent at the slower speed is longer than time spent at the faster speed.
Use total distance over total time: \(v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\).

label.en: ▲ Exam Pacing & Verification Strategy — Beyond AB — Core BC Topics Overview

body.en: High-Speed Exam Shortcut (College Board AP Calculus BC): When a linear system asks for a combined expression like \(3x + 3y\) rather than \(x\) and \(y\) individually, add or subtract the two equations directly before isolating either variable—this often yields the target expression in a single step.

question.en:
Level 1 · Foundations

Evaluate the improper integral \(\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^3}\,dx\) using proper limit notation, or state that it diverges.
question.ar:
Level 1 · Foundations

احسب قيمة the improper integral \(\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^3}\,dx\) using proper limit notation, or state that it diverges.

solution.en: Rewrite as a limit: \[ \lim_{b \to \infty} \int_1^b x^{-3}\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty} \left[ -\frac{1}{2x^2} \right]_1^b = \lim_{b \to \infty} \left( -\frac{1}{2b^2} - \left(-\frac{1}{2(1)^2}\right) \right). \] Since \(\lim_{b\to\infty} \frac{1}{2b^2} = 0\): \[ 0 - \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = \mathbf{\frac{1}{2}}. \] The integral converges to \(\frac{1}{2}\).
solution.ar:
خطوات الحل التفصيلية:

Rewrite as a limit: \[ \lim_{b \to \infty} \int_1^b x^{-3}\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty} \left[ -\frac{1}{2x^2} \right]_1^b = \lim_{b \to \infty} \left( -\frac{1}{2b^2} - \left(-\frac{1}{2(1)^2}\right) \right). \] Since \(\lim_{b\to\infty} \frac{1}{2b^2} = 0\): \[ 0 - \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = \mathbf{\frac{1}{2}}. \] The integral converges to \(\frac{1}{2}\).

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Medium — Planar Kinematics & Polar Area Geometry

body.en: Unit 9 expands single-variable motion along a line to two-dimensional motion in the Cartesian plane using parametric equations and vector-valued functions \(\vec{r}(t) = \langle x(t), y(t) \rangle\), alongside polar coordinates \(r = f(\theta)\).

1. Velocity, Speed & Acceleration:
• Position: \(\vec{r}(t) = \langle x(t), y(t) \rangle\)
• Velocity: \(\vec{v}(t) = \langle x'(t), y'(t) \rangle\)
• Speed (magnitude of velocity): \(s(t) = |\vec{v}(t)| = \sqrt{[x'(t)]^2 + [y'(t)]^2}\)
• Total Distance Traveled (Arc Length): \(L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{[x'(t)]^2 + [y'(t)]^2}\,dt\)
• Acceleration: \(\vec{a}(t) = \langle x''(t), y''(t) \rangle\)

2. Polar Coordinates & Sector Area:
• Polar to Cartesian: \(x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta, \quad r^2 = x^2 + y^2\)
• Polar Area: \[ A = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta [r(\theta)]^2\,d\theta. \]

label.en: Level 2 (Medium) — Worked Example · 2D Parametric Speed & Distance Traveled

body.en:
Problem: A particle moves in the \(xy\)-plane with velocity vector \(\vec{v}(t) = \langle 6t, 3t^2 - 3 \rangle\) for \(t \ge 0\). At \(t = 2\), compute the speed of the particle, and calculate the total distance traveled from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 2\).

Step 1 · Instantaneous Speed at \(t = 2\): \[ |\vec{v}(2)| = \sqrt{[x'(2)]^2 + [y'(2)]^2} = \sqrt{[6(2)]^2 + [3(4) - 3]^2} = \sqrt{12^2 + 9^2} = \sqrt{144 + 81} = \sqrt{225} = \mathbf{15}. \]

Step 2 · Total Distance Traveled Setup: \[ L = \int_0^2 \sqrt{(6t)^2 + (3t^2 - 3)^2}\,dt = \int_0^2 \sqrt{36t^2 + 9t^4 - 18t^2 + 9}\,dt. \] Simplify the radicand: \[ = \int_0^2 \sqrt{9t^4 + 18t^2 + 9}\,dt = \int_0^2 \sqrt{(3t^2 + 3)^2}\,dt = \int_0^2 (3t^2 + 3)\,dt. \]

Step 3 · Integration: \[ L = \left[ t^3 + 3t \right]_0^2 = (2^3 + 3(2)) - 0 = 8 + 6 = \mathbf{14}. \]

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium

Find the slope of the tangent line \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) to the polar cardioid \(r = 1 - \cos\theta\) at \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\).
question.ar:
Level 2 · Medium

أوجد ميل the tangent line \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) to the polar cardioid \(r = 1 - \cos\theta\) at \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\).

solution.en: Recall \(x = r\cos\theta\) and \(y = r\sin\theta\). By the Product Rule: \[ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta} = \frac{r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta}{r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta}. \] Given \(r = 1 - \cos\theta \implies r' = \sin\theta\). At \(\theta = \pi/2\): \(r = 1 - 0 = 1\), \(r' = 1\), \(\sin(\pi/2) = 1\), \(\cos(\pi/2) = 0\). Substitute: \[ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{(1)(1) + (1)(0)}{(1)(0) - (1)(1)} = \frac{1}{-1} = \mathbf{-1}. \]
solution.ar: Recall \(x = r\cos\theta\) and \(y = r\sin\theta\). بتطبيق Product Rule: \[ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta} = \frac{r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta}{r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta}. \] Given \(r = 1 - \cos\theta \implies r' = \sin\theta\). At \(\theta = \pi/2\): \(r = 1 - 0 = 1\), \(r' = 1\), \(\sin(\pi/2) = 1\), \(\cos(\pi/2) = 0\). عوّض: \[ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{(1)(1) + (1)(0)}{(1)(0) - (1)(1)} = \frac{1}{-1} = \mathbf{-1}. \]

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced / AP FRQ — Infinite Sequences, Power Series & Error Bounds

body.en: Unit 10 is the apex of AP Calculus BC. Students must master testing series for absolute and conditional convergence, constructing Taylor and Maclaurin polynomials, finding intervals of convergence with endpoint analysis, and bounding truncation errors.

1. Taylor Polynomial of Degree \(n\) Centered at \(x = c\): \[ P_n(x) = f(c) + f'(c)(x-c) + \frac{f''(c)}{2!}(x-c)^2 + \dots + \frac{f^{(n)}(c)}{n!}(x-c)^n = \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{f^{(k)}(c)}{k!}(x-c)^k. \]

2. Alternating Series Error Bound: If \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^{n+1} a_n\) satisfies the AST (terms strictly decrease in magnitude toward 0), then the truncation error after \(N\) terms is bounded by the magnitude of the first omitted term: \[ |S - S_N| \le a_{N+1}. \]

3. Lagrange Error Bound (Taylor's Remainder): If \(|f^{(n+1)}(t)| \le M\) for all \(t\) between \(c\) and \(x\), then: \[ |R_n(x)| = |f(x) - P_n(x)| \le \frac{M}{(n+1)!}|x - c|^{n+1}. \]

label.en: Level 3 (Advanced/FRQ) — Worked Example · Interval of Convergence with Endpoint Analysis

body.en:
Problem: Find the radius of convergence and interval of convergence for the power series: \[ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n (x + 3)^n}{n \cdot 4^n}. \]

Step 1 · Ratio Test for Radius: \[ L = \lim_{n\to\infty} \left| \frac{(x+3)^{n+1}}{(n+1)4^{n+1}} \cdot \frac{n \cdot 4^n}{(x+3)^n} \right| = \lim_{n\to\infty} \left( \frac{n}{n+1} \cdot \frac{|x+3|}{4} \right) = \frac{|x+3|}{4}. \] For absolute convergence, set \(L < 1\): \[ \frac{|x+3|}{4} < 1 \implies |x + 3| < 4 \implies \mathbf{R = 4}. \] The open interior is \(-4 < x + 3 < 4 \implies -7 < x < 1\).

Step 2 · Test Right Endpoint \(x = 1\): Substitute \(x = 1\): \[ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n (4)^n}{n \cdot 4^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{n}. \] This is the alternating harmonic series. By the Alternating Series Test, \(1/n > 0\), decreases, and \(\lim 1/n = 0\), so it converges. Thus \(x = 1\) is included: \([\dots, 1]\).

Step 3 · Test Left Endpoint \(x = -7\): Substitute \(x = -7\): \[ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n (-4)^n}{n \cdot 4^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n (-1)^n 4^n}{n \cdot 4^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}. \] This is the divergent harmonic \(p\)-series (\(p = 1\)). Thus \(x = -7\) is excluded: \((-7, \dots\).

Conclusion: The radius of convergence is \(\mathbf{R = 4}\), and the interval of convergence is \(\mathbf{(-7, 1]}\).

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced / AP FRQ

Let \(f(x)\) be a function whose third derivative satisfies \(|f'''(x)| \le 6\) for all \(x \in [0, 0.4]\). If the second-degree Taylor polynomial \(P_2(x)\) centered at \(c = 0\) is used to approximate \(f(0.2)\), find the maximum possible error in this approximation using the Lagrange Error Bound.
question.ar:
Level 3 · Advanced / AP FRQ

ليكن \(f(x)\) be a function whose third derivative satisfies \(|f'''(x)| \le 6\) for all \(x \in [0, 0.4]\). إذا كان the second-degree Taylor polynomial \(P_2(x)\) centered at \(c = 0\) is used to approximate \(f(0.2)\), أوجد maximum possible error in this approximation باستخدام Lagrange Error Bound.

solution.en: Using the Lagrange Error Bound formula with \(n = 2\), \(c = 0\), \(x = 0.2\), and \(M = 6\): \[ |R_2(0.2)| \le \frac{M}{(2+1)!}|x - c|^{2+1} = \frac{6}{3!}|0.2 - 0|^3. \] Since \(3! = 6\): \[ |R_2(0.2)| \le \frac{6}{6}(0.2)^3 = 1 \times 0.008 = \mathbf{0.008} \quad \left( \text{or } \frac{1}{125} \right). \] The maximum truncation error is guaranteed to be no greater than 0.008.
solution.ar: باستخدام Lagrange Error Bound formula with \(n = 2\), \(c = 0\), \(x = 0.2\), and \(M = 6\): \[ |R_2(0.2)| \le \frac{M}{(2+1)!}|x - c|^{2+1} = \frac{6}{3!}|0.2 - 0|^3. \] Since \(3! = 6\): \[ |R_2(0.2)| \le \frac{6}{6}(0.2)^3 = 1 \times 0.008 = \mathbf{0.008} \quad \left( \text{or } \frac{1}{125} \right). \] The maximum truncation error is guaranteed to be no greater than 0.008.
